title: Data visualization
summary: Chart one week of Larkhaven Bikes trips with ggplot2. Build a scatter plot, make it clear for every reader, and save it. Then try bar charts, histograms, boxplots, density curves and small multiples.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes ggplot2

steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` loads **ggplot2**, which draws every chart in this lesson. It also loads readr, for reading files, and the rest of the core tidyverse.

steps.title: A week of trips: read_csv() and glimpse()

runs.purpose: read one week of trips into `week`
runs.task: Read `data/trips-week.csv` into a variable called `week` with `read_csv()`.

runs.purpose: list `week`'s columns, with their types and first values

steps.explain:
`read_csv()` read {n_week} trips into `week`, **one row per trip**. They run from Monday 2 to Sunday 8 June 2025. Its message says which type it gave each column.

`glimpse()` lists the columns down the Console, each with its type and first few values:
- `<dbl>` for numbers, such as `distance_km`
- `<chr>` for text, such as `bike_type`
- `<dttm>` for date-times, such as `started_at`

Every chart in this lesson is drawn from these columns.

steps.title: Distance and duration: ggplot() and geom_point()

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = distance_km, y = duration_min)) +
  geom_point()
runs.purpose: plot each trip's duration against its distance
runs.task: Draw a scatter plot of `week`, with `distance_km` on the x-axis and `duration_min` on the y-axis. Use `ggplot()`, `aes()` and `geom_point()`.

steps.explain:
A ggplot2 chart has **three parts**:
- the **data**: `week`
- the **aesthetic mappings** in `aes()`, which say which column goes where: `distance_km` along the x-axis, `duration_min` up the y-axis
- the **geom**, which says how each row is drawn: `geom_point()` draws one point per trip, and `+` adds it to the chart

The points rise to the right, so **longer trips take longer**. The point furthest to the right is {max_km} km.

At any one distance, the points spread upwards: some riders take their time.

steps.title: Colour by bike type: mappings and settings

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = distance_km, y = duration_min, colour = bike_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
alternatives: ggplot(week, aes(distance_km, duration_min, color = bike_type)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(method = lm)
ggplot(week, aes(distance_km, duration_min)) + geom_point(aes(colour = bike_type), alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(aes(colour = bike_type), method = "lm")
runs.purpose: colour the trips by bike type, and add a straight line for each
runs.task: Draw the scatter plot again, with `colour = bike_type` added to `aes()` and the points at `alpha = 0.3`. Add a straight line for each bike type with `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`.

steps.explain:
`colour = bike_type` is **inside** `aes()`, so it's a **mapping**. Each point gets its colour from its trip's bike type, and ggplot2 adds a legend to say which is which.

`alpha = 0.3` is **outside** `aes()`, so it's a **setting**. Each point is only 30% solid, so you can see through it, and crowded areas look darker.

The colour mapping is in `ggplot()`, so **every layer uses it**. That's why `geom_smooth()` drew one straight line for each bike type. (The Console's message names its formula, `y ~ x`.) If you mapped the colour in `geom_point()` instead, only the points would be coloured, and there would be one line for all trips.

At 10 km, the classic line is at about {classic_10} minutes and the electric line at about {electric_10}. **E-bikes are faster.**

steps.title: Labels and colours for every reader: labs() and ggsave()

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = distance_km, y = duration_min, colour = bike_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "E-bikes cover the same distance faster",
    x = "Distance (km)",
    y = "Duration (minutes)",
    colour = "Bike type"
  )
alternatives: ggplot(week, aes(distance_km, duration_min, color = bike_type)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(method = 'lm') + labs(title = 'E-bikes cover the same distance faster', x = 'Distance (km)', y = 'Duration (minutes)', color = 'Bike type') + scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8)
runs.purpose: add a title and axis labels, and use colours every reader can tell apart
runs.task: Add `scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.8)` to the last chart. Then add `labs()` with title `"E-bikes cover the same distance faster"`, x `"Distance (km)"`, y `"Duration (minutes)"` and colour `"Bike type"`.
Save the chart as `distance-duration.png`, 7 by 5 inches, with `ggsave()`.

steps.explain:
`labs()` gave the chart a **title**. It also put words a reader understands in place of the column names, on the axes and the legend.

`scale_colour_viridis_d()` replaced ggplot2's default red and blue with colours from the **viridis** palette. People with the common kinds of colour blindness can tell these colours apart, and so can anyone reading a copy in black and white.

The `_d` is for *discrete* values, such as bike types. `end = 0.8` stops before the palette's palest yellow.

`ggsave()` saved the last chart drawn as `distance-duration.png`, 7 by 5 inches, in the project folder. You can see it in the **Files** pane.

steps.title: Counting categories: geom_bar()

runs.purpose: count the trips by member type
runs.task: Draw a bar chart of how many trips each `member_type` made, with `geom_bar()`.

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = member_type, fill = bike_type)) +
  geom_bar()
runs.purpose: split each bar by bike type
runs.task: Draw the bar chart again with each bar filled by `bike_type`.

steps.explain:
`geom_bar()` **counts the rows** in each category. So its y-axis, `count`, isn't a column of `week`: ggplot2 worked it out. Members made {n_member} of the week's trips, and casual riders made {n_casual}.

`fill = bike_type` splits each bar by a second category. This shows how the two categories relate: **a larger share of members' trips were on classic bikes**.

For bars, `fill` colours the inside. `colour` would only colour the outline.

steps.title: How long, and when: geom_histogram()

runs.purpose: show how long trips take, in two-minute bins
runs.task: Draw a histogram of `duration_min` with bins 2 minutes wide (`binwidth = 2`).

runs.purpose: show when trips start, hour by hour
runs.task: Draw a histogram of `started_at` with one bin per hour: `binwidth = 3600`, in seconds.

steps.explain:
A **histogram** shows how a number is spread out. It cuts the x-axis into bins, and counts the trips in each bin.

With `binwidth = 2`, each bar is two minutes wide. The tallest bar, from {peak_from} to {peak_to} minutes, is **the most common trip length**. The bars trail off to the right: a few trips last an hour or more.

`started_at` is a date-time, counted in seconds, so `binwidth = 3600` makes one bar per hour. Weekdays have **two peaks**, the morning and evening rush hours. Saturday and Sunday have one broad hump, from late morning to late afternoon. The gaps on Monday at 5 pm and Thursday around midday are hours when it rained.

*A different bin width can change the picture.* Too wide hides the shape, and too narrow turns it into noise.

steps.title: Comparing groups: geom_boxplot() and geom_density()

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = member_type, y = duration_min)) +
  geom_boxplot()
runs.purpose: compare members' and casual riders' trip durations with boxplots
runs.task: Draw a boxplot of `duration_min` for each `member_type` with `geom_boxplot()`.

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = duration_min, colour = member_type)) +
  geom_density()
runs.purpose: compare the same durations as density curves
runs.task: Draw density curves of `duration_min`, coloured by `member_type`, with `geom_density()`.

steps.explain:
Both charts compare a number across groups.

In a **boxplot**, the line across each box is the **median**: half the trips took less. It's {median_member} minutes for members and {median_casual} for casual riders. The box holds the middle half of the trips. The dots above it are unusually long trips.

A **density curve** is a smoothed histogram. Its area is always 1, so you can compare groups of different sizes. Members' curve peaks sooner and higher, and casual riders' curve spreads further to the right.

**Casual riders' trips take longer.**

steps.title: Small multiples: facet_wrap()

runs.code:
ggplot(week, aes(x = distance_km, y = duration_min, colour = bike_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~member_type)
alternatives: ggplot(week, aes(distance_km, duration_min, color = bike_type)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + facet_wrap(vars(member_type))
runs.purpose: draw the scatter plot again, one panel per member type
runs.task: Draw the scatter plot of `duration_min` against `distance_km` again, coloured by `bike_type`, with `alpha = 0.3`. Give it one panel per `member_type` with `facet_wrap()`.

steps.explain:
`facet_wrap(~member_type)` split the chart into **one panel per member type**, on the same axes. That way you can compare a third variable without crowding one chart.

Members' trips stay close to a line, and the longest took {max_member} minutes: they ride straight to where they're going. Casual riders' trips spread far above it, up to {max_casual} minutes.

In both panels, **e-bike trips sit below classic ones**.
